tldr: Without using human demonstrations or complex reward shaping, this reinforcement learning study achieves a 98.2% success rate across all 20 tasks on the challenging NIST Assembly Task Board #1 using a single policy trained solely on sparse binary rewards given upon assembly completion.
hero_caption: An overall view of the NIST Assembly Task Board #1 built in simulation. The 20 movable parts shown in yellow (pegs, gears, connectors, nuts, etc.) form diverse assembly tasks with completely different shapes and clearances.
overview:
Robotic assembly is a notoriously difficult problem because of complex contact dynamics and friction between parts. In particular, the standard benchmark "NIST Assembly Task Board #1 (ATB1)" features 20 distinct assembly pairs, ranging from thin peg insertions to millimeter-scale nut threading. Until now, no single learning-based method has solved all of these tasks. Prior work managed to tackle them only by using human demonstrations, manually designing detailed distance and orientation reward functions (reward shaping) for each task, or relying on scripted assembly primitives.

The authors looked to the history of the Go AI "AlphaGo Zero," which discovered superhuman play purely from win/loss rewards without human game records. They asked: in precision robotic assembly, could a robot spontaneously discover unexpected, dexterous strategies using only binary success rewards? At first glance, a sparse reward setting where feedback is given only when assembly is complete seems hopelessly difficult to explore. However, the authors took a counter-intuitive approach: train all 20 heterogeneous tasks simultaneously with a single policy, and explore at scale using GPU-parallel simulation.

Their experiments showed that a single policy reached an extremely high overall training success rate of 98.2% across all 20 tasks. This substantially outperformed specialist policies trained separately on individual tasks (81.4%), confirming positive transfer through shared experience. Furthermore, in long-horizon tasks assembling up to 10 parts in an unconstrained order within a single episode, planning-like behaviors emerged spontaneously without an explicit planner—such as clearing an obstacle out of the way or preparing one part, assembling another, and then returning to finish the first.
contributions: Developed the first single multi-task reinforcement learning policy to solve all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1 using only sparse binary rewards, without human demonstrations, reward shaping, or task decomposition.

Demonstrated that training diverse heterogeneous tasks simultaneously enables solving difficult parts that individual specialist policies failed to solve (such as the 4 mm peg and M4 nut), achieving an overall success rate of 98.2%.
Showed that a single policy can sequentially assemble up to 10 part pairs in a single episode without prescribed ordering or hierarchical planners.

Discovered that advanced dexterous manipulation skills not specified by humans—such as reorienting parts using contact with the environment, regrasping, and tapping nuts to thread them—emerge purely from binary rewards.

sections.heading: Bringing the AlphaGo Zero philosophy to robotic assembly: why binary rewards?
sections.summary: The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 is a long-standing challenge with 20 tasks featuring tight clearances and rich contacts. Inspired by AlphaGo Zero learning from game outcomes without detailed guidance, the authors tackled this benchmark using a single multi-task policy with sparse binary rewards and large-scale parallel RL.
sections.details:
Robotic assembly is in high demand in manufacturing, yet it remains exceptionally challenging. A primary benchmark is the "NIST Assembly Task Board #1 (ATB1)." It contains 20 assembly pairs, including peg insertion, gear meshing, various connector insertions, and nut threading. Solving them is difficult for three main reasons: first, there is no fixed sequence, and placing one part first can block access to the next; second, it requires long-horizon execution from picking parts up across wide initial poses to transporting and inserting them; and third, parts are as small as 4 mm in diameter with near-zero clearances, causing frequent jamming from contact and friction.

Prior learning-based methods aided exploration by starting from pre-grasped states, training separate policies per task, or hand-crafting dense progress rewards (reward shaping). However, this demands heavy manual engineering whenever new parts appear.

Here, the authors drew inspiration from "AlphaGo Zero." Just as superhuman moves emerged purely from game-ending win/loss rewards without human instruction, they hypothesized that robotic assembly could be solved solely with binary rewards indicating whether assembly is complete. The key insight was training diverse tasks with varying geometries and tolerances simultaneously under a single policy, rather than learning them in isolation. By using task diversity as a stepping stone for exploration, the method achieved a 98.2% success rate across all 20 tasks.

sections.heading: Limitations of prior work and the breakthrough AlphaNIST aimed for
sections.summary: This section reviews progress in large-scale simulation learning for contact-rich assembly and multi-task RL, highlighting how this work differs from prior methods. Its key novelty lies in scaling a single shared policy using only binary rewards, without complex reward engineering or task distillation.
sections.details:
### II-A Large-Scale Learning for Contact-Rich Assembly
Advances in GPU-parallel physics simulators (like PhysX and Newton) have enabled large-scale experience collection using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). Prior work such as Factory simulated nut threading across thousands of environments, and OmniReset demonstrated demonstration-free RL by diversifying initial states. Success-Guided Sampling (SGS) introduced efficient sampling based on success rates. However, all of these trained separate policies for each task. AlphaNIST adopts the sampling principle of SGS, but trains all 20 tasks together with a single multi-task policy.

### II-B Challenges in Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning
Typically, training diverse tasks simultaneously causes single-policy performance to degrade compared to individual learning (specialist policies) due to conflicting task gradients. Techniques like PCGrad (projecting conflicting gradients), PopArt (normalizing reward scales), or distilling from specialist policies have been proposed to mitigate this. AlphaNIST, however, uses a uniform binary criterion—assembly completion—which naturally eliminates reward scale mismatches, allowing standard PPO to succeed in multi-task learning with a remarkably simple setup.

### II-C Learning-Based Robotic Assembly
Conventional learning-based assembly split tasks into short local primitives like grasping and insertion, or relied on imitation learning and curriculum learning. For rewards, researchers typically added dense auxiliary terms measuring distance to grasp targets or target poses. However, such reward shaping can cause policies to fall into unintended local optima when part shapes or sizes change. AlphaNIST revisits whether terminal success verification alone can drive learning, just like in AlphaGo Zero.

sections.heading: Task formulation: a shared MDP using point clouds with no discrete task IDs
sections.summary: All 20 assembly tasks are formulated as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP). The policy receives no discrete task ID; it autonomously recognizes geometry from surface point clouds to decide its actions.
sections.details:
### III-A Task Definition and MDP
The 20 assembly pairs on ATB1 are formulated as multi-task reinforcement learning. Each task $e \in \mathcal{E}$ ($|\mathcal{E}|=20$) is defined by a movable part, its static receptacle, and a set of fully assembled target configurations.

At the start of an episode, a task and initial state pair $(e, s_0)$ is sampled from a distribution $\rho$. A critical design decision is that the policy $\pi_\theta$ does not receive a discrete task ID indicating which task is active. Instead, the observation $o_t$ includes surface point clouds of the movable part, the receptacle, and the robot itself. The policy must infer the situation purely from geometric visual input and proprioception (such as joint positions) to generate the appropriate assembly actions.

sections.heading: The AlphaNIST training framework: three pillars and distributed learning
sections.summary: The framework integrates three elements: cached diverse reset states, success-guided sampling (SGS), and binary rewards evaluating only assembly completion. Multi-GPU training was run on Isaac Lab with up to 256K parallel environments.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Reset State Coverage and Experience Allocation
The key to unlocking exploration is initial state diversity. Extending OmniReset, the authors built a bank of cached task ID and state pairs $(e_i, \bar{s}_i)$. This bank covers diverse phases: parts lying randomly on the table, already grasped in the air, positioned just before receptacles, and partially inserted. This allows the policy to work backward from difficult insertion phases to earlier stages.

For sampling from the bank, SGS Beta sampling is employed. Based on the recent episode success rate $\hat{p}_i$, states with intermediate success rates—representing the current learning frontier—are prioritized. This prevents wasting computational budget on states that are already mastered or still completely intractable.

### IV-C Binary Assembly Reward and Control Regularization
Only when the relative coordinates of each part fall within a threshold $\epsilon = 0.001\,\mathrm{m}$ (1 mm) of the target pose does the robot receive a success reward $r_t^{\mathrm{task}} = 1$, terminating the episode. Intermediate progress rewards are strictly zero. In addition, to protect hardware and encourage smooth motions, penalties (control costs) on action magnitude, joint velocities $\dot{q}_t$, and torques $\tau_t$ are applied with fixed coefficients $c$. This acts purely as motion regularization and provides no information about assembly progress.

### IV-D Shared Policy and Robot Control
Isaac Lab is used as the simulator, modeling a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda robot with a parallel gripper. The control frequency is $25\,\mathrm{Hz}$, and the policy outputs relative joint position commands and gripper open/close commands. The network architecture adopts SimBa, well-suited for point cloud processing, configured separately for actor and critic without parameter sharing.

### IV-E Distributed Training and Scaling
The training algorithm uses standard PPO with 4K environments per GPU, scaling up to 256K parallel environments in synchronous training. A simple data-parallel scheme averages gradients gathered across GPUs to update parameters.

sections.heading: An astonishing 98.2% success rate and emergent assembly skills
sections.summary: A single policy achieved a 98.2% success rate across all 20 tasks, outperforming individual specialist policies (81.4%). In addition, binary rewards alone induced regrasping, tapping motions, and planning-like behaviors that sequentially assemble 10 parts.
sections.details:
### V-A Positive Transfer from Simultaneous Heterogeneous Training
In comparative experiments across 64K environments over 25K iterations, the single shared policy trained with sparse binary rewards reached a 98.2% average success rate across all 20 tasks. In contrast, specialist policies trained individually on each task averaged only 81.4%. On micro-part tasks like M4 nut threading, 4 mm peg insertion, and thin rod insertion, specialist policies collapsed to success rates below 0.3%, whereas the shared policy solved them reliably. Grasping and insertion experiences from other parts transferred positively to these difficult components.

In terms of compute, the shared policy completed training in 410 GPU hours, whereas the specialist policies consumed 16.1K GPU hours combined—roughly 39.3 times more resources. Furthermore, a shared policy trained with dense distance and orientation reward shaping plummeted to 17.8%. Because each geometry requires a different intermediate pose, fixed dense rewards hindered exploration.

### V-B Scaling and Sampling Effects
Scaling parallel environments from 1K to 256K improved the success rate of binary rewards with Beta sampling monotonically from 38.6% to 97.4%. Beta sampling also demonstrated clear superiority over uniform sampling (84.3%).

### V-C Emergent Skills in Short Horizons
Without human demonstration, sophisticated dexterous skills emerged spontaneously. For example, after lifting a peg by its center, the robot recognized that it could not fully insert it, dropped it intentionally, and regrasped it near the end. On the M4 nut, the fingers rhythmically tapped one side to rotate it and engage the threads.

### V-D Long-Horizon Multi-Pair Sequential Assembly
In experiments assembling up to 10 parts in a single episode—where rewards were withheld until all parts were simultaneously assembled—the policy succeeded at sequential assembly. Without an explicit planner, it demonstrated spontaneous planning and coordination: staging a distant USB connector nearby, assembling a rod in the meantime, and then returning to insert the connector.

sections.heading: Looking ahead from simulation to real-world robots
sections.summary: All findings currently remain in simulation, meaning robustness against real-world sensor noise and contact modeling errors must still be validated. In addition, completing all 20 parts on the board in a single episode will require further efficiency improvements.
sections.details:
A primary limitation of this work is that all experiments were conducted in simulation. Although realistic Franka Panda velocity limits, torque limits, and friction parameters were incorporated, overcoming camera perception noise, control latencies, and contact discrepancies (the sim-to-real gap) requires real-robot validation in future work.

Additionally, while sequential assembly succeeded for up to 10 pairs within a single episode, the policy has not yet solved all 20 pairs on the board simultaneously. Solving all 20 pairs solely with terminal binary rewards involves an even vaster exploration space, demanding further improvements in simulation throughput and RL algorithms.

sections.heading: Takeaway: task diversity is what builds general dexterity
sections.summary: AlphaNIST proves that for complex assembly tasks, dispensing with human priors and reward engineering in favor of binary rewards and large-scale parallel RL yields superhuman dexterity and planning behaviors. It shows a new path: don't avoid task diversity—use it as a resource.
sections.details:
In robot learning, conventional wisdom held that when tasks are too complex, one must decompose them and guide the policy with human priors. AlphaNIST challenges this assumption. It demonstrates that with sufficient state coverage and large-scale parallel RL, sparse binary rewards alone are enough for rich contact skills and long-horizon staging behaviors to emerge.

Solving diverse tasks with different shapes and tolerances at the same time is not an obstacle; it is a powerful stepping stone toward conquering difficult tasks. This discovery offers valuable insights for robot foundation models and manipulation research. It marks a crucial step toward general-purpose assembly systems where robots discover optimal strategies through their own trial and error, rather than through tedious human tutoring.

takeaways: Heavily engineered reward shaping tends to cause local optima during multi-task learning, whereas clear binary completion rewards perform dramatically better at scale.

Challenging tasks (such as micro-part insertion and threading) are solved much more easily through positive transfer when trained alongside diverse tasks in a single policy than when learned in isolation.
Pairing diverse reset states (OmniReset) with sampling focused on intermediate success rates (SGS) enables long-horizon exploration from sparse rewards without demonstrations.
Without any hierarchical high-level planner, a low-level control policy alone can spontaneously acquire planning-like coordination, such as staging one part and assembling another first.
limitations: All results are obtained within Isaac Lab simulation; sim-to-real transfer to physical robots (evaluating perceptual noise and contact modeling errors) has not yet been demonstrated.
Sequential assembly within a single episode succeeded for up to 10 pairs, but scaling to complete all 20 board pairs in one continuous episode remains unachieved.
